messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Weber, a 42-year-old American combat pilot who had previously done relief transport work in a war zone, spoke about the defining incident as something she both knew in detail and could hardly tell. During one winter deployment she was assigned to fly supplies and evacuate civilians from an area where shelling had pushed families onto frozen roads. What stayed with her was the cold first: the way the air bit through her gloves on the tarmac, the white breath, the metallic sound of nearby vehicles idling while frightened civilians crowded toward transport. There had been car engines revving and stopping in irregular bursts, people shouting, and a night in which she woke after only a few hours to another emergency call. Now, when she tries to describe what happened, she often stops and says she cannot find words for the worst part. At other moments she can recount it in a flat, almost detached way, as if she is talking about someone else, yet the images themselves come back with a sharpness that feels more real than ordinary life.

Since returning home, seemingly ordinary sensations pull her straight back into that state. A cold gust walking across the airfield to her aircraft, the sound of cars outside a parking structure, or the residue of a nightmare on waking can bring up the same vivid fragments with unnerving force. Those moments do not feel like remembering in the usual sense; they feel immediate, sensory, and more real than the kitchen or hangar around her. Because the memories arrive in flashes she cannot fully organize into words, they also leave her with the conviction that something fundamental was broken there, beyond explanation. When she is hit by the sound of traffic or wakes with the taste of a dream still on her, she is overcome not only by images but by the thought that the world no longer works by any rules she once trusted.

Over time Elena had come to believe that the deployment had stripped life of meaning and taken away the person she used to be. She described feeling as if her old beliefs about safety, purpose, and competence had been destroyed. That sense of identity loss feeds the way she remembers: when she looks back, she either goes numb, as though the event belongs to a stranger, or she is confronted by vivid shards that seem to confirm that the person who lived before the war zone is gone. Out of that bleakness she spends hours blaming herself—telling herself she should have done more, seen more, prevented more—and when the self-reproach becomes unbearable she buys things online late at night for a brief sense of relief. She also avoids films, television, and news coverage about conflict or displacement because she feels she cannot bear what those images say about the world now.

The memories have also changed how she moves through daily life. When vivid fragments are stirred, she becomes intensely alert, listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering the house and waking in the night to check doors and windows. Strangers approaching her in ordinary places—at a gas station, in a grocery parking lot, even near the base—feel dangerous before she has time to think. The more she lives in this state of readiness, the more the world appears hostile and senseless, reinforcing her sense that her assumptions have been shattered. That vigilance makes her exquisitely sensitive to cues around her; she notices every car sound outside, every shift in temperature, and any jolt awake from sleep becomes the kind of moment in which she braces for danger before she is even fully conscious.

At work the pattern is especially visible. As a pilot, she cannot avoid cold mornings on the flight line or the constant hum and backfire of vehicles around the base. She has begun taking longer routes to the aircraft to avoid congested service roads, and after bad nights she lingers in her car before going in, trying to settle herself. At home she keeps the television off if there is any chance of war footage, but the avoidance narrows her world and leaves her alone with the same fragments she is trying not to stir. The rumination that follows—hours of circling self-blame—seems only to strengthen the memories, making them return later with even greater vividness. Her impulsive spending briefly distracts her, yet the parcels arriving at the house become another sign, to her, of how unlike herself she has become. And the more time she spends scanning the house and sleeping lightly, the easier it is for dream residue, cold air, or passing cars to set the whole sequence off again.

By the time Elena sought help, her marriage was strained by her nighttime checking and her emotional distance, and she was frightened by how little of her old sense of purpose remained. She came in after waking from another nightmare and finding herself already on her feet, listening for an intruder, unable to shake the feeling that home was not safe. What frightened her most was not only the memories themselves, but the possibility that they meant the world was permanently ruined and that she had permanently become someone she no longer recognized. What she hoped, cautiously, was that she might learn how to live in her own life again without bracing at every sound.
